newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Filipinas fear for future in Hong Kong.
newsitem.headline: Filipinas fear for future in Hong Kong.

text.p: Thousands of Filipina maids fear for their future in Hong Kong after the British colony is handed over to China at the end of this month.
They worry that Chinese women from the mainland will take their jobs at much lower wages and deprive them of a vital financial lifeline to their families back in the Philippines.

Both Chinese President Jiang Zemin and Hong Kong's future ruler Tung Chee-hwa have sought to reassure the 140,000 Filipinas there will be no change in the status quo after July 1. But those pledges have fallen on deaf ears.

"We are all worried about the handover. We are thinking about moving to Canada or Taiwan or Singapore," said 25-year-old Jhona, one of thousands of Filipinas who congregate every Sunday in Hong Kong's Statue Square.
The central district grinds to a halt for their one day off a week. Police cordon off the streets as women spill out from underpasses and crouch under umbrellas in the rain.

The Filipinas, enjoying an impromptu fiesta beneath the towering skyscrapers of the city's big banks, give each other pedicures, swap magazines and exchange photos. The constantly chattering women are called The Sparrows of Statue Square.
Jhona, a nurse from Subic Bay, works for a Chinese family and looks after their two young children of nine and seven.
Space is always at a premium in this human anthill that is home to 6.4 million people. "I share a room with the older boy. We both have bunk beds."

The Hong Kong government sets minimum standards for domestic helpers. They have a two-year contract with free room and board, minimum pay of about US$500 a month and one week's holiday a year. Authorities make spot checks to prevent abuses.
But tales of exploitation still abound.
"Some Filipinas are not given enough food. Some even sleep in the kitchen on folding beds," said Jhona, who regularly sends money back to the Philippines for her sister's education.
Their monthly remittances account for a major chunk of the country's gross domestic product each year.
Connie, a 32-year-old who has not seen her two children for three years, said: "I too am worried about the future. The Chinese family I first worked for were very demanding.

"I slept on a sofa in the sitting room. I started work at five in the morning and did not finish sometimes till two the next morning. I am talking to my auntie in Toronto and she is going to help me find work there."

With the community of 25,000 Britons dropping, jobs with western families are now limited. The Filipinas fear Chinese mainlanders, speaking Cantonese and ready to work for low wages, could undercut them. "They are cheaper," said Jhona.

Despite the carnival atmosphere of a square packed with women determined to have a good time on their one and only day off, there is an undercurrent of worry, loneliness and above all the constant heartache of separation.
Connie wistfully confessed: "My children write and call me all the time but sometimes I am sad and feel very homesick."
